title: Transaction scale changes the measured incidence of US tariffs
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 34901, Did Foreigners Pay America's Tariffs? Quantity Discounts, Scale Economies and Incomplete Pass-Through
geography: United States trade; 2018-2019 US tariffs and transaction-level imports

denominator.unit: administrative transaction-level US import microdata; abstract does not disclose the full transaction or product count

quantity_discounts.value: Transaction-level quantity discounts are pervasive in US trade

discount_mechanism.value: Observed discounts reflect transaction-level scale economies rather than market power

incidence_boundary.value: Tariff incidence depends on shipment scale and transaction structure, not only the posted tariff rate

observations.method: Administrative microdata analysis of US import transactions, quantity discounts, shipment scale, and tariff pass-through.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract does not disclose the full transaction universe, product coverage, confidence intervals, or household-price mapping; transaction prices are not identical to retail shelf prices.
observations.subgroup: Import transactions of different sizes, foreign exporters, US importers, downstream producers, retailers, and consumers exposed to affected goods.
observations.counterinterpretation: Scale economies can coexist with bargaining power or market power; finding a cost mechanism does not rule out strategic pricing or unequal bargaining across firms.

denominator.unit: tariff-affected import transactions in administrative microdata

observed_pass_through.value: Observed import prices rose one-for-one with the 2018-2019 US tariffs
observed_pass_through.unit: reported price response relative to tariff change

transaction_scale.value: Transaction sizes collapsed after the tariffs

measurement_puzzle.value: The loss of scale economies explains the apparent one-for-one import-price response

observations.method: Decomposition of observed tariff-era import-price changes into strategic pass-through and transaction-scale effects.
observations.uncertainty: The result concerns import prices and does not directly establish final consumer prices, quantities purchased, retailer margins, or welfare; tariff exposure and shipment-scale changes may be correlated with broader trade adjustment.
observations.subgroup: Importers and exporters changing shipment size, with downstream exposure varying by product and supply chain.
observations.counterinterpretation: Other changes in sourcing, composition, exchange rates, inventory, or product quality could contribute to the observed import-price movement.

denominator.unit: percent of the tariff change used as the pass-through base

scale_free_pass_through.unit: percent of the tariff increase passed through to scale-free import prices

foreign_exporter_absorption.value: Foreign exporters absorbed a significant share of the tariff burden through reduced markups

consumer_link.value: The import-side incidence estimate is an upstream condition for consumer-price exposure, not a direct household-price estimate

observations.method: Pass-through estimate controlling for micro-level scale economies in transaction size.
observations.uncertainty: The 60 percent estimate is conditional on the paper's scale adjustment and 2018-2019 tariff setting; the abstract does not identify downstream retail pass-through, household incidence, or whether exporter markups recover later.
observations.subgroup: Foreign exporters, US importers, downstream firms, and consumers along supply chains with different transaction scales.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reduced exporter markups may reflect temporary scale loss, renegotiation, or product reallocation rather than a stable distribution of tariff burden; downstream firms may still pass costs forward.

related_sources.claim: Official NBER landing page with the transaction-level quantity-discount, scale-economy, one-for-one observed-price, and 60 percent scale-free pass-through findings.
NBER DOI route for the working paper.
Existing project control for connecting tariff incidence, shipment scale, firm adjustment, and household price exposure.

boundary: This record adds an upstream US trade-incidence counterexample: apparent one-for-one tariff pass-through can partly reflect lost transaction scale, while scale-adjusted pass-through is 60 percent and foreign exporters absorb a significant share through lower markups. It does not establish retail prices, household incidence, welfare, employment, or a universal tariff mechanism.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official NBER W34901 page reviewed for transaction-level quantity discounts, scale economies, one-for-one observed import-price movement, collapsed transaction size, 60 percent scale-free pass-through, and exporter markup absorption.
